JSON: Name: bionic_adaptive_fmcw_lidar Title: Integrated electro-optic-comb based adaptive parallel FMCW LiDAR for region-selective high-resolution 4D machine vision Short Hypothesis: Dynamically concentrating a fixed budget of electro-optic-comb-derived FMCW channels onto selected regions of interest by tuning the external-cavity laser center wavelength and comb repetition rate will increase local point density by at least 2× and reduce local ranging RMSE by at least 25% relative to uniform global scanning using the same total number of channels and acquisition time. Related Work: Existing LiDAR approaches include single-channel mechanical scanners that trade temporal throughput for angular resolution, dense replicated-channel arrays (e.g., large VCSEL/receiver arrays) that scale hardware, and parallel-comb or dual-comb systems that provide simultaneous multi-wavelength probing but suffer from limited adaptive tunability, processing load, or chirp bandwidth constraints. Fourier-domain/FDML and Kerr-microcomb multiplexing enable multi-wavelength projection but typically use fixed spectral patterns or face dispersion- and Raman-limited chirp linearity, which prevents rapid ROI reconfiguration. Optical phased arrays and acousto-optic beamsteerers offer non-mechanical steering but add control complexity and have limited efficiency or field-of-view tradeoffs. Coherent FMCW detection provides unambiguous range and velocity per channel, yet implementations that provide both chip-scale integration and dynamic per-ROI allocation of sensing resources remain undeveloped. Multi-sensor fusion with cameras improves semantic context but is limited by coarse LiDAR sampling and calibration sensitivity. Abstract: We address the trade-off between whole-field coverage and localized high-resolution sensing in LiDAR by proposing an integrated coherent frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) architecture that adaptively concentrates sensing resources on regions of interest. The system combines an agile external-cavity seed laser with on-chip electro-optic frequency comb generators and a dual-polarization coherent receiver to produce mutually coherent, frequency-chirped multi-wavelength probe channels whose spectral positions and repetition rates are reconfigured in real time. By reallocating a fixed set of parallel channels to selected angular- spectral bands, the architecture decouples local angular resolution from total physical channel count, enabling higher point density and concurrent per-channel velocity and reflectivity measurement. The main contributions are (1) a chip-scale pipeline for dynamic electro-optic-comb generation synchronized with laser tuning for ROI-focused FMCW probing; (2) multi-heterodyne dual-polarization coherent reception and frequency-domain channel separation for simultaneous range/velocity retrieval; and (3) an experimental evaluation showing quantifiable improvements in local resolution and 4D scene reconstruction while preserving overall scanning throughput. Expected outcomes are demonstrable 4D-plus imaging with reduced hardware scaling and increased adaptability for autonomous perception. Experiments: Datasets and scenes: (A) Controlled laboratory scenes: calibrated static roadboard with targets (traffic cone, box, barricade), variable depth targets, and moving objects (pendulum and thrown sphere) for velocity ground truth; (B) Outdoor driving-like sequences using recorded vehicle trajectories from KITTI-like sequences (synchronized camera + LiDAR emulation) for calibration/generalization; (C) Synthetic ray-traced point-cloud scenes for large-scale param sweeps. Baselines: (1) Uniform global-scan FMCW using identical total optical power and same number of physical RF amplifiers but without dynamic comb repetition or ECL wavelength tuning (i.e., fixed spectral distribution); (2) Mechanical high-resolution single-channel scanner matched for point density in ROI but with equal hardware time budget; (3) Parallel comb approach with fixed channel allocation (no adaptive reallocation); (4) Variant without dual-polarization reception (single polarization). Evaluation metrics: local point density (points per deg^2) in ROI, angular resolution (deg), ranging RMSE (cm) in ROI and global RMSE, velocity RMSE (m/s), per-frame processing latency (ms), end-to-end throughput (points/s), SNR/reflectivity dynamic range (dB), and power consumption (W). Experimental setup: hybrid integrated platform with ECL + TFLN electro-optic combs, SiN/SiPh coherent dual-polarization receiver, diffraction/grating vertical dispersion and galvo/polygon horizontal scanning. Acquire matched-duration frames across methods; maintain equal total emitted optical power and equal acquisition time per frame. Parameter sweep & ablation: (i) Vary comb repetition rate to adjust ROI granularity: test repetition rates corresponding to channel spacings {20.4, 21, 38, 43.6} GHz and measure point density and RMSE; (ii) Vary number of parallel comb lines used for probing (1, 9, 54, 150 effective lines) to assess scaling; (iii) Ablation A: disable ECL wavelength tuning and emulate ROI by beam steering only; Ablation B: disable dual-polarization receiver; Ablation C: replace electro-optic combs with fixed Kerr-microcomb-like spectral pattern. Comparisons: report relative improvement ratios (density and RMSE) between adaptive method and each baseline, and latency/resource overhead for real-time FFT and channel separation. Statistical reporting: run n>=10 repeated captures per configuration; report mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence intervals. Risk Factors and Limitations: Chirp nonlinearity and unequal comb-line amplitude (non-flat comb envelope) causing channel-dependent ranging bias; loss of mutual coherence between comb generators under temperature or mechanical drift leading to degraded multi-heterodyne demultiplexing; limited ECL tuning speed and thermal MRR tuning rate restricting real-time ROI reallocation frequency; optical amplifier gain spectrum and available output power limiting usable number of comb lines and maximum range; polarization-mode dispersion and alignment causing reduced SNR in one polarization channel and biased reflectivity estimates; signal processing and FPGA/SoC compute bottlenecks for real-time FFT and per-channel peak detection at high channel counts; calibration sensitivity for LiDAR–camera fusion producing reprojection errors under vibration or misalignment; scaling to long-range outdoor scenarios impeded by eye-safety constrained emitted power and sunlight-induced background noise; fabrication variability in TFLN/SiN/SiPh integration affecting device yield and repeatability; robustness limits in adverse weather (rain, fog, snow) where coherent detection and scattering reduce effective performance.
